narrative:
The model has assessed your loan application and concluded that you represent a significant credit risk. Specifically, it predicts a 38% probability that you would become a bad credit risk, meaning there is roughly a one-in-three chance you would fail to repay the loan. This level of risk is above what the bank is willing to accept, so your application was denied.

The most important factor driving this decision was the status of your checking account. Your account is currently overdrawn, with a balance below zero. This is uncommon among approved borrowers—only about 13% of them have an overdrawn account. A negative balance signals current financial stress, and this weighed heavily against your application.

The second and third most influential features actually helped you. Your savings situation—unknown or no savings—did not hurt your application; in fact, it slightly lowered your risk score compared to other applicants. Similarly, the purpose you gave for the loan, listed as "others," had a small positive effect, making you appear less risky than if you had chosen a more typical purpose.

However, these favorable factors were not enough to counterbalance the negative signal from your overdrawn checking account. The model ultimately saw the overall risk as too high.

What should you do next? The most effective step is to improve your checking account situation. Bring your balance to at least zero and keep it positive for several months. This directly addresses the main factor that led to the denial. Continue maintaining your good credit history—you have paid all previous credits at this bank—and consider reapplying after you have stabilized your account. Building a small savings cushion could also strengthen your application further.
